I have been farming these 11.6 mu for 30 years, since I came to this village at 25. I never went to school, not even one day. Everything I know I learned from my mother-in-law, from watching old Zhang across the road, and from doing it myself year after year. My son works in a factory in Shijiazhuang and sends money home, but the land is still what feeds us. I have my husband and my daughter-in-law to help, and we hire a few days of labor at harvest if we are desperate.

This year I will split my land the same as last year. I have 8 mu where I do wheat and then maize, one crop after another. That is my main field — it puts food on the table and corn in the feed bin. Then 3 mu I plant cotton. The cotton price at the buyer last year was not bad, so I keep it. The last 0.6 mu is a small corner plot near the house where I plant mungbean for eating at home and selling a few jin in the village.

For the wheat on those 8 mu: I buy the improved wheat seed from the dealer in town, the kind in the red bag. I use 35 jin per mu. In October I hire the rotary tiller man to go over the field — he charges 50 yuan per mu. For fertilizer, I put one big bag of that 15-15-15 compound fertilizer per mu as base. That bag is 100 jin. I know it is a lot, but last year when I tried to save money and used less, the wheat came up thin and yellow and I lost face. I would rather spend the money and have a full crop. Then in March when the wheat turns green and stands up, I spread 30 jin of urea per mu. When the wheat is shooting up tall, I spread another 30 jin of urea per mu. I irrigate three times from the well: once before winter if the ground is dry, once when the wheat is getting tall, and once when the heads are forming. I spray twice — once for weeds right after sowing, and once in spring for the bugs that eat the leaves. If the weather is decent like last year, I expect 1000 jin per mu.

For the summer maize on the same 8 mu: As soon as the wheat is cut in June, I do not waste time tilling. I plant the hybrid maize seed directly into the wheat stubble, the kind called nongda something — I buy it by the package, about 5 jin per mu. At sowing I put one bag of that high-nitrogen compound fertilizer per mu, the yellow bag the dealer says is for corn. That is 100 jin per mu. I irrigate twice — once right after planting if the rain does not come, and once when the maize is up to my waist. I spray twice — herbicide once, and once for the worms that bore into the stalk. I expect about 1200 jin per mu.

For cotton on the 3 mu: I plant the improved cotton seed, about 3 jin per mu. I hire the rotary tiller for this field too because cotton likes the soil soft. I put one big bag of compound fertilizer per mu when I plant, and another half bag when the yellow flowers open. Cotton is hungry and the bolls will drop if you are stingy. I irrigate three times and I spray four times — those aphids and bollworms never stop. I hope for 500 jin of seed cotton per mu.

For mungbean on the 0.6 mu: I use the seed I saved from last year, the small green ones. I do not buy new seed — that is wasting money for such a small plot. I put about 20 jin of compound fertilizer on the whole plot. I water it once from the well and spray once for bugs. I expect about 120 jin total from that little corner.

I do what I did last year. Change is dangerous. If old Zhang puts one bag per mu, I put one bag per mu. If I spend too much on fertilizer, that is just money. If the crop fails, that is a disaster.

decision.reasoning_summary: I farm 11.6 mu the same way I did last year because change is risky. I put 8 mu into wheat-maize rotation, 3 mu into cotton for cash, and 0.6 mu into mungbean for home use. I copy what my successful neighbors do: one bag of compound fertilizer per mu for wheat, maize, and cotton, with extra urea topdressing on wheat and cotton. I irrigate from my well and spray when I see bugs. I would rather spend too much on fertilizer than risk a thin crop, but I still save seed for mungbean and skip tilling for maize to save time and money.
